video_title: The New Rules for Founders | Garry Tan on a16z
gist: YC president Garry Tan argues the per-seat SaaS model and its 10-20x forward-revenue multiple are already broken, that the new unit of labor is a markdown skill file run on a cron (enabling ~$15M ARR in four months with two or three people), and that founders should spend $50-100k/year token-maxing on harnesses like Open Claw to 'live in 2028'. His counter-consensus twist: bureaucracy and human working-memory limits will stretch this transition over ~20 years, so incumbents like Microsoft keep their moats - which he calls the white pill.

insights.claim: Garry Tan says a pure per-seat SaaS business is 'not totally clear it will exist in another 5 or 10 years' and is now only acceptable as a wedge toward a data or network-effect moat.
insights.speaker: Garry Tan
insights.so_what: Directly challenges the terminal-value assumption under most seat-based software comps; favors positioning toward outcome-priced or data-moat businesses.
insights.quote: a pure like per seat SaaS thing, like not totally clear it will exist in another 5 or 10 years. Like it's perfectly fine as a wedge, but if you're doing that now in 2026, like you better hope that that's like a leap to some sort of moat

insights.claim: The 10-20x next-twelve-months revenue multiple that was treated as an 'iron law' for SaaS two years ago has already stopped being true, according to Tan.
insights.speaker: Garry Tan
insights.so_what: A named-and-dated repricing of the standard software valuation heuristic from the president of YC; watch forward-revenue multiple compression in seat-based software comps.
insights.quote: SaaS was God, you know, like the 10 20X like next 12 months uh revenue multiple was like, you know, iron law. And like it's hard to believe it was like, oh yeah, no, that's not true at all now.

insights.claim: Tan cites companies going from zero to roughly $15M ARR in about four months with two or three people plus a few hundred agent skill files, implying revenue-per-employee ratios that break conventional startup benchmarks.
insights.speaker: Garry Tan
insights.so_what: If replicable, it collapses the capital and headcount required per revenue dollar and undermines burn-multiple and headcount-based diligence norms.
insights.quote: you can go from zero to 15 mil ARR in about 4 months with like two or three people and like hundreds of agent like, you know, a few hundred skill files.

insights.claim: Tan argues the historic YC requirement for co-founders is weakening because vibe coding and agentic coding let one person be a multiple of themselves, though he still believes co-founders are net positive all else equal.
insights.speaker: Garry Tan
insights.so_what: Signals that a top accelerator's screening criteria are shifting toward solo founders, widening the fundable founder pool.
insights.quote: for the longest time we really really believed that you needed co-founders and I think that everything else being equal, having co-founders is net really really good.

insights.claim: Tan's operating model is that any business process should be done once perfectly and then converted into a markdown file plus code plus tests that can be re-run on a cron, making 'a markdown file an employee'.
insights.speaker: Garry Tan
insights.so_what: A concrete, copyable template for where agentic labor substitution actually lands inside a company's cost structure.
insights.quote: a markdown file is an employee.

insights.claim: Tan says the same skillification loop applies across sales, marketing, customer support and every other function, not just engineering.
insights.speaker: Garry Tan
insights.so_what: Widens the addressable displacement well beyond dev tools into every SG&A line item.

insights.claim: The failure mode of agent-built systems is not intelligence but data hygiene: once you accumulate many markdown/skill files you need provenance, conflict resolution favoring the more recent fact, and a sweeping cron job for accuracy.
insights.speaker: Garry Tan
insights.so_what: Points to memory/provenance/context-governance tooling as the bottleneck layer worth funding rather than raw model capability.
insights.quote: that's where like provenance matters. That's where um conflict management sort of you know when you have two facts if you have provenance then you're like well this is the more recent one like this is the one that wins.

insights.claim: Building agentic systems reduces to iteratively finding the current bottleneck and instructing the agent to build the software or markdown file that removes it; Tan found himself automated down to only doing black-box verification.
insights.speaker: Garry Tan
insights.so_what: Describes the practical ceiling of current agent autonomy - human residual is verification - which is where the next tooling gap sits.

insights.claim: Tan built G Stack, G Brain and Garyslist.org himself, distilling recorded YC office hours into a markdown script for raising founder ambition that he had to ask Claude to weaken by 90% before open-sourcing.
insights.speaker: Garry Tan
insights.so_what: Shows senior investors now build their own agent tooling; also a rare look at YC's advising IP being productized.
insights.quote: I actually had to go into Claude, and I said, "Reduce this by 90%. Reduce the strength and intensity of this prompt by 90%."

insights.claim: Tan embedded a 'please apply to YC' message inside his open-source agent tooling that only surfaces to top-decile Claude Code users judged by product and design thoughtfulness, using open source as an agentic deal-sourcing funnel.
insights.speaker: Garry Tan
insights.so_what: A novel top-of-funnel mechanic - open-source instrumentation as founder-scouting - that other funds will likely copy.
insights.quote: But only if you're a top 10% user of Claude code.

themes.theme: Token maxing and the coming harness wars

insights.claim: Tan claims the consumer frontier products (ChatGPT, Claude) are deliberately compute-constrained, so getting full-strength intelligence requires self-hosted harnesses like Open Claw or Hermes Agent tuned to load 800k-1M tokens per request.
insights.speaker: Garry Tan
insights.so_what: Implies a durable gap between shipped consumer capability and raw model capability - and a market for harness/context layers on top of the labs.
insights.quote: the frontier model labs that are, you you know, letting you use ChatGPT or Claw, I think that they're still pretty constrained on and pretty constrained on, um, amount of compute they want to give you.

insights.claim: Tan estimates it costs roughly $50,000-$100,000 per year to run agents at full strength on every request, and argues that for a CEO or founder this is worth it because it lets you 'live in 2028' today.
insights.speaker: Garry Tan
insights.so_what: Quantifies the price of a capability arbitrage window; also a rough floor on what premium agentic seats could eventually be priced at.
insights.quote: it costs, I don't know, 50 or 100,000 dollars a year to like use the agents at full strength, like full 150 IQ on every request.

insights.claim: Tan predicts 2027 will be 'the harness wars', with a fight for a billion consumers that only starts once today's frontier compute drops to roughly $50-100, effectively restarting the browser wars.
insights.speaker: Garry Tan
insights.so_what: Dates the consumer AI land-grab to 2027-2029 and ties its trigger to a specific cost threshold investors can track.
insights.quote: My guess is like next year, 2027, will be like the harness wars.

insights.claim: Tan expects today's frontier pure-model compute to cost about 50 or 100 dollars in two or three years, making cost - not capability - the current gate on consumer AI.
insights.speaker: Garry Tan
insights.so_what: A concrete cost-decline curve to test; the crossing point is when free-to-try consumer AI products become viable.
insights.quote: it's really a cost thing. Like, it's just too expensive right now,

insights.claim: The a16z host frames a barbell in token economics: price per token of the frontier trends toward infinity while the price per token of last week's frontier model collapses to zero, which is what will unlock free-to-try consumer AI.
insights.speaker: host
insights.so_what: A clean mental model for why consumer AI margins improve on a lag and why fast-follower model tiers, not frontier, will carry consumer distribution.
insights.quote: the price per token of frontier is going to infinity. Like, my thesis is infinity dollars a token, you can't have it. And the price per token of the model that was frontier a week ago is collapsing to zero.

insights.claim: The host argues consumer AI is dramatically underbuilt relative to the primitives available, calling it a tragedy that no one has shipped ambitious consumer products despite computers being emotive for the first time in 40-50 years.
insights.speaker: host
insights.so_what: Flags consumer AI as the underinvested category relative to enterprise/agentic tooling - a stated a16z appetite.
insights.quote: We have these magical primitives. Like, we have computers that are emotive and have emotional texture for the first time in 40 or 50 years. What a tragedy that we haven't built more ambitious consumer products yet.

insights.claim: Tan expects the next computer to be voice-first with deep memory, built on computer use, diarization and ingestion, converging on a benevolent assistant that knows a user's hopes, fears and desires.
insights.speaker: Garry Tan
insights.so_what: Names the specific capability stack (computer use, memory, diarization, ingestion) where the consumer assistant race will be won.
insights.quote: it's pretty clearly going to be voice.

insights.claim: Tan publicly revises his own timeline: converting to Open Claw convinced him agentic transformation would happen immediately, and he now believes that view was 'not correct at all'.
insights.speaker: Garry Tan
insights.so_what: A prominent AI bull explicitly extending his adoption timeline - relevant to anyone underwriting near-term agentic revenue.
insights.quote: I was convinced that like being becoming a convert to open claw made me very very convinced that it was going to happen right away and then at this point I'm like that's not correct at all.

themes.theme: Institutional slowness as the white pill

insights.claim: Tan's counter-consensus take is that bureaucracy, middle management and human cognitive limits will slow AI diffusion so much that the transition takes about 20 years - and he frames that slowness as good news, not a problem.
insights.speaker: Garry Tan
insights.so_what: Argues against both the doom case and the fast-disruption case; supports incumbents' terminal values and lengthens the runway for displacement trades.
insights.quote: society is way slower than you think. Government is way slower than you think. Every company in the world is way slower than you think.

insights.claim: Tan says explicitly that startups will not replace incumbents like Microsoft because there are real structural moats, calling this antithetical to what most of Silicon Valley says.
insights.speaker: Garry Tan
insights.so_what: The head of YC arguing incumbent moats hold is a notable data point against the 'AI kills the incumbents' short thesis.
insights.quote: there are real motes to these things. Like there are structural reasons why a Microsoft isn't going anywhere.

insights.claim: Tan's core diagnostic for why institutions are unready is that the entire world - business, government, products - is designed around humans who can only hold seven plus or minus two things in their head, while a human plus an agent can hold the equivalent of three Harry Potter books.
insights.speaker: Garry Tan
insights.so_what: A reusable screen for which processes get disrupted first: anything whose design constraint was human working memory.
insights.quote: the world is basically built on things that are built around human beings and human beings can only keep seven plus or minus two things in their head at any given time.

insights.claim: Tan notes YC's Startup School drew 7,000 attendees, mostly 18-22 year olds who became adults during ChatGPT, and argues society will run on their expectations in roughly 20 years - the mechanism behind his slow-diffusion timeline.
insights.speaker: Garry Tan
insights.so_what: Generational turnover, not model capability, is his rate-limiter for AI adoption - a testable framing for adoption forecasts.
insights.quote: we had 7,000 people. Most of them were 18 to 22 years old.

insights.claim: Tan and the host frame the last century of managerial science as possibly a 100-year detour from founder mode, with the implication that agents restore direct founder control and cut intentional work to one to three days a week.
insights.speaker: host
insights.so_what: If management layers are the compressible cost, the displacement lands on middle management rather than individual contributors.
insights.quote: maybe that was a 100-year distraction from what was founder mode

insights.claim: Tan's Microsoft anecdote - carrying a baseball bat to the Windows team to get a P3 bug fixed across seven org levels - is his canonical example that big-company coordination failure, not talent, is the waste, and that a startup can and must organize differently.
insights.speaker: Garry Tan
insights.so_what: The mechanism behind his incumbent-inertia thesis: coordination cost is the incumbent tax startups arbitrage.
insights.quote: An org like Microsoft can't. [music] Yes, but a startup can. Yes, and every startup must.

themes.theme: Agentic management and erasing the API line

insights.claim: Brex's Pedro runs agents over meeting transcripts from all his direct reports to see two levels down, detect what is broken and who is in conflict, and walk into meetings he was never in with perfect three-week context.
insights.speaker: Garry Tan
insights.so_what: A live enterprise use case for agentic org observability - a category with obvious demand from CEOs and obvious HR/compliance friction.
insights.quote: he can use uh meetings that he's not in now to figure out like what's broken, what's in conflict, like who's who's in conflict with who.

insights.claim: Brex solved the safety objection to running Open Claw in a highly regulated fintech by open-sourcing a supervisory layer called Craptrack - an agent that watches all network traffic and actions of the agent.
insights.speaker: Garry Tan
insights.so_what: Agent-supervision/observability layers are the unlock for regulated-industry agent adoption - a fundable wedge.

insights.claim: Tan identifies management failure - the business becoming too big to fit in one person's head - as a defining reason startups and businesses fail, and argues agents plus memory plus retrieval give a CEO ground-truth 'clairvoyance' rather than filtered opinion.
insights.speaker: Garry Tan
insights.so_what: Reframes agents as a scaling-limit remover for founder-led companies, which raises the ceiling on how far founder mode can scale.
insights.quote: the business becomes too big to fit in one person's head.

insights.claim: Tan argues AI erases Venkatesh Rao's 'API line' - the divide between those who command APIs and those who serve them - citing YC company Kolabtree shipping a bug-report endpoint built for agents that replies in real time with a triage verdict and a workaround.
insights.speaker: Garry Tan
insights.so_what: Agent-to-agent commercial interfaces are an emerging product surface; also a bullish reframe for labor below the API line.
insights.quote: I actually think AI erases the API line.

insights.claim: Tan invokes the Toyota Production System - letting the line worker change the line because they hold the most context - as the model for where agents should sit, implying the middle organizing layer rather than the executive or the individual contributor.
insights.speaker: Garry Tan
insights.so_what: A specific prediction about which org layer agents absorb first: PM-style coordination work, not direction-setting or execution.
insights.quote: if you are the person doing the work on the line, you should be allowed to change the line because you are the person with the most amount of contacts

insights.claim: The host argues agents let organizations run conflicting approaches in parallel and unbundle conflict from human emotion, which is why decentralized organizations and economies outperform - every idea gets tried.
insights.speaker: host
insights.so_what: Suggests a testable operating advantage: agent-run parallel exploration as a replacement for consensus-driven roadmapping.

themes.theme: Founder selection: late bloomers and the 35-45 cohort

insights.claim: Tan identifies a mega-trend of 35-45 year old repeat founders who know what to build, citing Peter Steinberger, and argues agents let one such person outperform an entire department at a Mag 7 company.
insights.speaker: Garry Tan
insights.so_what: Contradicts the young-founder prior that dominates seed investing; experienced-operator-plus-agents may be the highest-alpha founder profile.
insights.quote: if you take that person like suddenly there's 400 of those people like you can outperform an entire department of like any mag seven.

insights.claim: Tan says agency and taste are now 'off the charts important' and are practiced rather than innate, positioning his own career of corrected mistakes as evidence against the fixed-high-agency-population view the host raises.
insights.speaker: Garry Tan
insights.so_what: Bears on whether AI tooling broadens the founder funnel or just amplifies the same top 20% - the host's explicit challenge.
insights.quote: suddenly agency and taste like off the charts important now

insights.claim: Tan's repeated career error - leaving web programming in 2003 because the web was declared dead, then turning down Peter Thiel's offer to co-found Palantir for a Microsoft level-60 promotion - is his evidence that following consensus over direct knowledge is the dominant destroyer of returns.
insights.speaker: Garry Tan
insights.so_what: The canonical opportunity-cost story behind YC's 'don't LARP' doctrine; useful lens on why consensus-chasing kills option value.
insights.quote: That was like a $2 billion to $4 billion mistake at this point.

insights.claim: Tan says 'what's hot and what should I work on' is the wrong question and the right one is what you uniquely know - the operating principle behind his 'don't LARP' meme at Startup School.
insights.speaker: Garry Tan
insights.so_what: A selection heuristic worth applying to founder pitches: unique first-party knowledge over thematic fit.
insights.quote: that's the wrong question to ask. Like the right question is like, "What are you interested in? What do you know uniquely?"

insights.claim: Tan's pattern-match for a great opportunity is that it looks like a toy on the fringe of the idea maze and you cannot find the intellectual edge of the conversation about it.
insights.speaker: Garry Tan
insights.so_what: A concrete screen for early-stage sourcing: unfindable intellectual edge as a positive signal.
insights.quote: a good measure of how interesting the thing is is can you find the edge?

insights.claim: Tan says everything that has worked in his life is 'kind of a cult' - a belief that flies in the face of orthodoxy - and that first-party investigation produces knowledge that published sources do not.
insights.speaker: Garry Tan
insights.so_what: Explains the contrarian-conviction filter he applies to companies; relevant to reading YC's selection behavior.
insights.quote: everything that's awesome in my life is kind of a cult.

themes.theme: SF civic turnaround as an exportable playbook

insights.claim: Tan says his political activation came from Asian Americans being roughly 25% of San Francisco's voting populace and 30% of the population while facing a DA ignoring crimes against elders and a school board hostile to middle-school algebra access.
insights.speaker: Garry Tan
insights.so_what: Explains the voting bloc mechanics behind SF's political shift - a template for how tech capital organizes politically in other cities.
insights.quote: Asian Americans are 25% of the voting populace about 30% of the population

insights.claim: Tan estimates 10-20% of San Francisco residents work directly in tech, arguing the industry is a large enough bloc to determine local outcomes if it participates.
insights.speaker: Garry Tan
insights.so_what: Quantifies the political leverage of the tech constituency in SF - relevant to housing, crime and permitting policy risk.
insights.quote: we're 10 20% of the people are like directly working in tech.

insights.claim: Tan's stated thesis is that everything is downstream of media and that institutional failure - specifically local TV declining to cover anti-Asian crime - is what let SF governance derange, so accountability must target media as well as government.
insights.speaker: Garry Tan
insights.so_what: Explains why tech figures are investing in owned media channels; Garyslist.org is the direct product of this belief.
insights.quote: everything is downstream of media at that point.

insights.claim: Tan is explicitly building Garyslist.org as an agentic newsroom to export the SF civic playbook to LA, New York, Minneapolis and Seattle - blue cities are the intended expansion market.
insights.speaker: Garry Tan
insights.so_what: A named vehicle and city list for tech-aligned local political organizing over the next cycle.
insights.quote: San Francisco should be the beacon for pushing this back in every blue city in America

insights.claim: Tan argues fixing local government mechanically fixes state and national over a five to ten year horizon because winners rise through a functional system, and that human coordination - not intelligence - is the binding constraint on civic problems.
insights.speaker: Garry Tan
insights.so_what: Frames where politically active tech capital will be deployed: municipal races rather than national.
insights.quote: if we fix local like state and national will fix itself

insights.claim: The host suggests AI ambition should be localized rather than copying an American template, citing the NHS as an example of what another country could target with the same technology.
insights.speaker: host
insights.so_what: Points to sovereign/public-sector AI deployments outside the US as an under-served category.
insights.quote: you don't have to have an American vision for how AI impacts your society. If you want the NHS to be incredible then like you can do that with this technology.
